newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Clinton urges greater effort to fight terrorism.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges greater effort to fight terrorism.

text.p: President Bill Clinton called on Tuesday for greater efforts to fight terrorism, singling out Iraq, Iran and Libya as countries that did not belong in the family of nations.
In an address to the General Assembly, he recalled asking U.N. members last year to commit themselves to a "goal of zero tolerance for aggression, terrorism and lawless behaviour."

"Frankly, we have not done that yet. Real zero tolerance means giving no aid and no quarter to terrorists who slaughter the innocent and drug traffickers who poison our children, and to do everything we can to prevent weapons of mass destruction from falling into the wrong hands," Clinton said.

Real zero tolerance required isolating states "that refuse to play by the rules we have all accepted for civilised behaviour," he added. "As long as Iraq threatens its neighbours and people, as long as Iran supports and protects terrorists, as long as Libya refuses to give up the people who blew up Pan Am (Flight) 103 (over Lockerbie, Scotland), they should not become full members of the family of nations."
Iran's seats in the Assembly hall were empty during Clinton's speech.

Clinton said the United States was pursuing a three-part strategy against terrorism: working more closely with like-minded nations, giving U.S. law enforcement agencies the toughest counterterrorism tools available and doing everything possible to make its airports and aircraft even safer.
He also called for a "no-sanctuary pledge, so that we can say with one voice to the terrorists, criminals and drug traffickers, 'You have no place to run, no place to hide.'"
He urged all U.N. members to sign 11 international conventions that would help prevent and punish terrorism and criminalize the use of explosives in terrorist attacks.

Calling for efforts to reduce the demand for drugs and take drugs off the streets, Clinton said the United States would do its part. Next week, he said, he would target more than $100 million worth of military equipment, services and training to Mexico, Colombia and other South American and Caribbean countries for the fight against drugs.
He also asked every nation that exported the chemicals needed to make illict drugs to create an informal group to deny those chemicals to drug producers.
"We must not let more drugs darken the dawn of the next century," Clinton added.
